3.1 Genotypes names to rename vcf file

vcf.names <- "xclude/genotype_names.txt" %>% 
  read.csv(header = F, col.names = "name_old") %>% 
  mutate(pmatch = toupper(name_old)) %>% 
  mutate(match = gsub(".*A(.+)_F.*", "\\1", pmatch)) %>% 
  select(!pmatch)

geno.names <- "genetics/genotype-names.csv" %>% 
  read.csv() %>% 
  unite(match, c(plots, crossn, line), remove = F, sep = "_") %>% 
  mutate(name_new = case_when(
    cross %in% c("SAL", "PAN", "HUA", "KCA", "COL", "BDJ", "CHU", "AYR", "CHO", "PAS") ~  as.character(paste(cross, line, crossn, sep = "_"))
    , TRUE ~ as.character(paste(cross, line, sep = "_"))
  )) %>% 
  select(match, name_new) %>% 
  distinct(name_new, .keep_all = T)

vcf.rename <- merge(vcf.names, geno.names, by = "match", all.x = T) %>% 
  mutate(name_new = case_when(
    is.na(name_new) ~ name_old
    , TRUE ~ name_new
  )) %>% 
  select(!match) %>% 
  mutate(name_new = gsub("KCA", "KAN", name_new)) %>% 
  mutate(name_new = gsub("COL", "NCO", name_new))

tab <- vcf.rename %>% 
  distinct(name_new)

9.7 LD decay

# vcf to bed

plink2 \
    --vcf genetics/pops/nam_SAL.vcf \
    --allow-extra-chr \
    --double-id \
    --make-bed \
    --out genetics/pops/SAL
    
plink2 \
    --vcf genetics/pops/nam_KAN.vcf \
    --allow-extra-chr \
    --double-id \
    --make-bed \
    --out genetics/pops/KAN

# LD calculation

plink2 \
    --bfile genetics/pops/SAL \
    --allow-extra-chr \
    --r2-unphased \
    --ld-window 99999 \
    --ld-window-kb 10000 \
    --ld-window-r2 0 \
    --out genetics/pops/SAL_LD

plink2 \
    --bfile genetics/pops/KAN \
    --allow-extra-chr \
    --r2-unphased \
    --ld-window 99999 \
    --ld-window-kb 10000 \
    --ld-window-r2 0 \
    --out genetics/pops/KAN_LD


##----------------------------
## Read LD files
##----------------------------

ld_sal <- read_table("genetics/pops/SAL_LD.vcor",
                     show_col_types = FALSE) |>
    mutate(pop = "SAL")

ld_kan <- read_table("genetics/pops/KAN_LD.vcor",
                     show_col_types = FALSE) |>
    mutate(pop = "KAN")

ld <- bind_rows(ld_sal, ld_kan)

##----------------------------
## Distance
##----------------------------

ld <- ld %>% 
    mutate(distance = abs(POS_B - POS_A))

##----------------------------
## Remove different chromosomes
##----------------------------

ld <- ld %>% 
    filter(`#CHROM_A` == CHROM_B)

##----------------------------
## Create bins
##----------------------------

bin_size <- 50000   # 50 kb

ld <- ld %>% 
    mutate(bin = floor(distance/bin_size)*bin_size)

##----------------------------
## Mean LD
##----------------------------

ld_summary <- ld %>% 
    group_by(pop, bin) %>% 
    summarise(
        mean_r2 = mean(UNPHASED_R2, na.rm = TRUE),
        median_r2 = median(UNPHASED_R2, na.rm = TRUE),
        n = n(),
        .groups = "drop"
    ) %>% 
    filter(n >= 50)

ggplot(ld_summary,
       aes(bin/1000,
           mean_r2,
           colour = pop))+

    geom_line(linewidth = 1.2)+

    geom_hline(yintercept = 0.2,
               linetype = 2)+

    labs(x="Physical distance (kb)",
         y=expression(r^2),
         colour="Population")+

    theme_classic(base_size = 14)

11.1 SALCEDO NAM

pheno <- fb %>% 
  filter(grepl("SALx", line))

vcfdt  <- "genetics/pops/nam_SAL.vcf" %>% 
  vcfR::read.vcfR()

info <- vcfdt %>% 
  vcfR::getFIX() %>% 
  as.data.frame() %>% 
  mutate(across(ID, ~ gsub("_", "",. ))) %>% 
  rowid_to_column()

chr <- info %>% 
  as.data.frame() %>% 
  mutate(chrome = gsub(".*([0-9]+[A-Z]+).*", "\\1", CHROM)) %>% 
  group_by(chrome) %>% 
  summarise(n = n()) %>% 
  deframe()
  
gwsdt <- vcfdt %>% 
  extract.gt() %>% 
  as.data.frame() %>% 
  mutate(across(everything(.), ~ case_when(
    . %in% "1/1" ~ 2
    , . %in% "0/1" ~ 1
    , . %in% "1/0" ~ 1
    , . %in% "0/0" ~ 0
  ))) %>% 
  rownames_to_column() %>% 
  arrange(rowname) %>% 
  pivot_longer(!rowname, names_to = "geno", values_to = "col") %>% 
  pivot_wider(names_from = "rowname", values_from = "col") %>% 
  separate(geno, c("family", "line"), remove = F) %>% 
  dplyr::select(!line) %>% 
  mutate(fam = case_when(
    family %in% "SALxPAN" ~ 1
    , family %in% "SALxNCO" ~ 2
    , family %in% "SALxHUA" ~ 3
  ), .after = family) %>% 
  merge(., pheno, by.x = "geno", by.y = "line")

rsl <- (length(gwsdt) - 11):length(gwsdt) %>% map(\(x) {
  
  trait <- gwsdt[x]
  
  nam_gwas = gwas(y = trait
                , gen = gwsdt %>% dplyr::select(starts_with("SNP_"))
                , fam = gwsdt$fam
                , chr = chr
                )
  
  plot(nam_gwas, alpha = alpha_bon
         , main = names(trait)
         ) %>% print
  
  nam_gwas$PolyTest %>% mutate(trait = names(trait)) %>% 
    rownames_to_column("ID")
  
})

  bind_rows() %>%

12.3 Itinerations

run_iteration <- function(trait, rep, data = phenotyping4gp) {
  # Split 60/40
  split_data <- initial_split(data, prop = 0.6)

  pheno_train <- training(split_data) %>% as.matrix()
  pheno_valid <- testing(split_data)  %>% as.matrix()

  geno_train <- imputed_markers[row.names(pheno_train), ]
  geno_valid <- imputed_markers[row.names(pheno_valid), ]

  # Modelo GBLUP con rrBLUP
  response <- mixed.solve(
    y = pheno_train[, trait],
    Z = geno_train,
    K = NULL,
    SE = FALSE,
    return.Hinv = FALSE
  )
  
  e <- as.matrix(response$u)
  response_predic <- as.vector((geno_valid %*% e)[, 1]) + as.numeric(response$beta)

  # Accuracy
  acc <- cor(response_predic, pheno_valid[, trait], use = "complete")
  
  # Normalized Root Mean Square Error (NRMSE)
  rmse <- sqrt(mean((pheno_valid[, trait] - response_predic)^2, na.rm = TRUE))
  nrmse <- rmse / sd(pheno_valid[, trait], na.rm = TRUE)

  tibble(
    trait = trait,
    replication = rep,
    ntrain = nrow(pheno_train),
    nvalid = nrow(pheno_valid),
    accuracy = acc, # range: [-1 to +1]
    nrmse = nrmse # range: [0, >1] where: 0 high precision accuracy
  )
}

ABSTRACT
Quinoa (Chenopodium quinoa Willd.) is a stress-tolerant pseudocereal recognized for its nutritional value and adaptation to marginal environments. However, breeding progress for yield and resilient cultivars remains constrained by limited knowledge of the genetic architecture of agronomic traits. To address this gap, two nested association mapping (NAM) populations were developed using the recurrent parents Salcedo INIA, a high-yielding cultivar, and Kancolla, a traditional highland landrace, crossed with four diverse founder cultivars from the Peruvian Altiplano. title: INTRODUCTION
text:
Plant material and population development
In a previous study on quinoa breeding [24], we developed six segregating populations derived from biparental crosses of traditional Peruvian cultivars to establish two nested association mapping (NAM) populations. A structured multi-parental design was implemented using two contrasting recurrent parents: Salcedo INIA (SAL) and Kancolla (KAN). The SAL-based panel was generated by crossing Salcedo INIA with three founder lines – Huariponcho (SAL × HUA), Pandela Rosada (SAL × PAN), and Negra Collana (SAL × NCO) – while the KAN-based panel comprised crosses between Kancolla and Huariponcho (HUA × KAN), Pasankalla (PAS × KAN), and Negra Collana (NCO × KAN). The F₁ progenies were advanced through five generations of selfing using a bulk method to increase homozygosity, producing 96 recombinant inbred lines (RILs) per cross. From these, 25 lines per population were selected and subsequently evaluated from the F₇ to F₉ generations in multi-location field trials across the Peruvian highlands to assess agronomic performance, yield stability, and adaptation under contrasting environmental conditions (Figure 1).






Figure 1: Breeding scheme for nested association mapping (NAM) using two populations developed for a quinoa breeding program in the Peruvian highlands. Two recurrent parents were used: Salcedo INIA (SAL) and Kancolla (KAN). SAL was crossed with Huariponcho (SALxHUA), Pandela Rosada (SALxPAN), and Negra Collana (SALxNCO), while KAN was crossed with Huariponcho (HUAxKAN), Pasankalla (PASxKAN), and Negra Collana (NCOxKAN).



Parental lines were selected based on agronomic performance, phenotypic divergence, and adaptation to Andean highland environments [24]. Salcedo INIA is a widely used cultivar characterized by high yield potential and resistance to frost and powdery mildew [25], and has also been studied for its postharvest physical properties and grain quality at different altitudes [26]. In contrast, Kancolla is a traditional landrace noted for its cold and hail tolerance and elevated saponin content [27]. It was identified as a resilient genotype in field trials in the Andean highland and in stressful environments such as saline soils and arid conditions of the Sahara desert [24,28]. The founder lines Huariponcho, Pandela Rosada, Pasancalla, and Negra Collana were chosen to maximize allelic diversity, capture adaptive variation, and enhance recombination within each NAM panel.

title: INTRODUCTION
text:
Phenotypic evaluation
Phenotypic data used in the present study were obtained from Lozano-Isla et al. [24]. The study generated BLUEs and BLUPs from multi-environment trials using mixed linear models. In the present study, the published BLUE values were used as phenotypic information. Field trials conducted at two experimental sites in the highlands of the province of Puno, Peru, near Lake Titicaca and approximately 40 km apart: Camacani (3,825 m a.s.l.) and Illpa (3,820 m a.s.l.). Phenological and agronomic traits were measured at three developmental stages: flowering (BBCH stage 69), physiological maturity (BBCH stage 89), and harvest (BBCH stage 99), according to the BBCH scale adapted for quinoa [29]. Standard descriptors developed by Biodiversity International [30] were employed to record traits, including days to 50% flowering (days), days to physiological maturity (days), plant height (cm), stem diameter (cm), panicle length (cm), panicle width (cm), grain yield per plant (g) and yield per plot (g/5 m2). Grain yield per plant was estimated using two subsamples of 10 randomly selected plants per experimental unit to ensure representative sampling. Panicle width × length (cm2) was included as a trait due to its correlation with yield [24].
Phenotypic data were subjected to quality control, including outlier detection and residual diagnostic analyses to verify model assumptions. Following the recommendations of Kozak and Piepho [31], residual plots were used to assess normality and homogeneity of variance. These procedures were performed and reported in our previous study [24], from which the BLUE estimates used in the present work were obtained.

title: INTRODUCTION
text:
Genotyping and sequence processing
DNA extraction and sequencing
Young leaves were sampled from three-month-old field-grown plants at Camacani. For each line, pooled tissue from two plants was dried in silica gel and shipped to the University of Hohenheim (Germany) for DNA extraction using the AX Gravity DNA kit (A&A Biotechnology, Poland). DNA integrity was assessed by agarose gel electrophoresis, and concentration was quantified using Qubit fluorometry (Qubit™ 4 Fluorometer, Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA). Whole-genome sequencing was conducted at Novogene (Beijing, China) using the Illumina NovaSeq S4 platform, generating 2 × 150 bp paired-end reads.
Read processing, variant calling, and SNP filtering
Raw sequencing reads from the 235 retained samples were processed using Trim Galore v0.6.7 [32] with parameters –paired and -q 30 to remove low-quality bases. High-quality reads were aligned to the quinoa reference genome (QQ74; CoGe ID 60716) using BWA-MEM v0.7.17 [33]. Resulting BAM files were sorted and indexed with SAMtools v1.8 [34], and duplicate reads were removed using Picard tools (http://broadinstitute.github.io/picard/). Variant calling was performed using BCFtools v1.11 [35]. Variants with more than 50% missing genotypes were filtered out using the expression F_MISSING > 0.5.
Subsequently, SNP filtering was conducted using the snpR R package [36], following the recommendations of Hemstrom et al. [37]. This included removal of non-polymorphic loci and application of thresholds of min_ind = 0.5 and min_loci = 0.75, with stratification by cross (facet = cross).

title: INTRODUCTION
text:
Population structure and genetic diversity
Population structure and genetic diversity indices were estimated using the snpR R package [36]. Genotype data were saved and imported into a VCF format as an snpRdata object using import.snpR.data() and then filtered using filter_snps() under population-specific faceting. Principal component analysis (PCA) was performed via plot_clusters() to visualize genetic stratification among lines. Ancestry inference was performed using sparse nonnegative matrix factorization (sNMF) within plot_structure(), testing K values from 2 to 10. The optimal K value was selected based on the minimization of cross-entropy, as recommended for high-dimensional genomic datasets. Genetic diversity indices - observed heterozygosity (H₀), expected heterozygosity (He), inbreeding coefficient (FIS) and the proportion of polymorphic loci - were calculated using calc_ho(), calc_he(), calc_fis() and calc_prop_poly(). Population differentiation was assessed via pairwise Weir and Cockerham’s FST, estimated via calc_pairwise_fst() and visualized as heatmaps.

title: INTRODUCTION
text:
Genome-wide association study
Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) were conducted to identify SNP–trait associations underlying yield-related traits in the quinoa NAM populations. To maximize statistical robustness and reduce spurious associations, multiple complementary statistical models were implemented in the rMVP R package [38]. The framework was selected because it is memory-efficient, visualization-enhanced, and parallel-accelerated, allowing efficient variance component estimation and large-scale computation. The fixed and random model circulating probability unification (FarmCPU) was used in the analysis [39]. This model combines fixed and random effects while correcting for population structure and kinship, thereby increasing statistical power across loci of varying effect sizes. To control for confounding, the first principal components derived from genome-wide SNP data were included as fixed covariates, while a kinship matrix was incorporated as a random effect. Significance thresholds were determined using Bonferroni threshold for the p-value where Bonferroni=m/; m=0.05 and is the number of SNPs (Supplementary File 1). This multi-model and multi-threshold strategy ensured both sensitivity in detecting true associations and stringency in minimizing false positives. The phenotypic data for the analysis was performed using the BLUEs calculated in the MLT in the second stage from Lozano-Isla et al [24] according to Holland & Piepho [40].

title: INTRODUCTION
section: Identification of candidate genes associated with significant SNPs
text:
Identification of candidate genes associated with significant SNPs
The genomic regions associated with significant SNPs identified in the genome-wide association analysis were further explored to identify potential candidate genes. The physical positions of the significant SNPs were used to define candidate genomic regions in the quinoa reference genome [41]. Genomic windows were defined around each lead SNP to capture nearby genes potentially associated with the trait. A window of ±100 kb around each significant SNP was used to delimit candidate regions.
Gene annotation was obtained from the Chenopodium quinoa reference genome (QQ74) available in the CoGe database (Genome ID 60716; https://genomevolution.org/coge/GenomeInfo.pl?gid=60716). The genome annotation file in GFF3 format was imported and processed in R using the packages GenomicRanges [42] and rtracklayer [43] to manipulate genomic coordinates (Supplementary File 1). Significant SNPs were converted into genomic range objects and expanded to the defined window size. Genomic overlaps between SNP windows and annotated gene coordinates were then identified using interval-based queries, allowing the detection of genes located within each candidate region. For each overlapping feature, gene identifiers and genomic coordinates were extracted to compile a list of candidate genes associated with each significant SNP.

title: INTRODUCTION
text:
Genomic prediction
Genomic prediction was implemented using the genomic best linear unbiased prediction (GBLUP) framework, which is widely used in plant breeding due to its reliability, scalability, and interpretability [44]. Marker effects were modeled across the genome using ridge regression BLUP (rrBLUP) [45], allowing the estimation of genomic estimated breeding values (GEBVs) under the assumption of predominantly additive genetic effects. This linear mixed model framework has been widely adopted in genomic selection because it captures a substantial portion of the genetic variance while remaining computationally efficient in high-dimensional datasets [46].
To assess predictive ability, cross-validation (CV) was used. In each replicate, 60% of the lines were randomly assigned to the training set for model fitting, while the remaining 40% were allocated to the validation set for prediction. To strengthen the robustness and reproducibility of accuracy estimates, this cross-validation procedure was repeated across 300 resampled prediction sets, each consisting of five independent CV iterations. This resampling strategy has been recommended in recent genomic prediction studies to ensure stable and unbiased evaluations of predictive performance [44].
Prediction accuracy was quantified with the Pearson correlation between observed phenotypes and genomic estimated breeding values (GEBVs) in the validation set, complemented by the normalized root mean square error (NRMSE) to account for scaling effects [47]. The Pearson correlation (r), which ranges from −1 to 1, measures the ability of the model to correctly rank genotypes according to their genetic merit, with values closer to 1 indicating higher predictive ability [48]. In contrast, the NRMSE quantifies the magnitude of prediction error relative to the scale of the trait, where values closer to cero indicate greater predictive precision [49].

title: INTRODUCTION
text:
Genetic structure and diversity
To assess the structure and differentiation of each NAM population, principal component analysis (PCA) and population structure analyses were performed, and the fixation index (Fst) was estimated to quantify the degree of population differentiation between both NAM populations (Figure 2). Additionally, diversity indices were calculated for each population, including proportion of polymorphic loci, observed heterozygosity (Ho), expected heterozygosity (He), and the inbreeding coefficient (FIS).
Low-coverage whole-genome sequencing of 348 lines generated a total of 361.95 Gb of raw data. Quality control at the sample level identified 113 samples with sequencing output below 50 Mb, which were excluded from further analyses. The remaining 235 samples yielded an average of 1.54 Gb per sample, corresponding to approximately 1.06× coverage of the 1.45 Gb quinoa genome [41] (Supplementary Figure 1). After filtering using BCFtools, initial dataset of 396,949 SNPs across the retained samples. At the final stage, filtering by families using snpR R package subset of 125 individuals was retained, resulting in a dataset of 6,046 high-quality SNPs used for subsequent genetic analyses (Supplementary Figure 2).
Principal component analysis (PCA) revealed clear genetic differentiation between the two NAM populations derived from the parental varieties Kancolla (KAN) and Salcedo INIA (SAL) (Figure 2 a). The first principal component (PC1), explaining 13.97% of the total variance, separated individuals according to parental origin, with KAN-derived genotypes clustering on the left and SAL-derived genotypes on the right. In contrast, the second principal component (PC2), accounting for 3.05% of the variance, did not reveal a clear pattern of differentiation between groups.
To elucidate the genetic structure and patterns of admixture among biparental families derived from KAN and SAL parental lines, the number of ancestral clusters (K) was inferred using sparse non-negative matrix factorization (sNMF). The number clusters for population structure was inferred for K = 2–10 (Supplementary Figure 3), which identified a stable structure at K = 3 based on the minimum mean cross-entropy criterion (Figure 2 b). Across K values, a primary subdivision aligned with parental background (KAN vs. SAL) was consistently recovered, with cross-specific admixture superimposed on this axis. At K = 3, KAN-derived families (NCO×KAN, HUA×KAN, PAS×KAN) were assigned predominantly to Cluster 2 (blue), with PAS×KAN showing the highest homogeneity (near-fixed membership), HUA×KAN displaying intermediate admixture, and NCO×KAN exhibiting the greatest admixture, including contributions from Clusters 1 and 3, and the largest overlap with SAL-derived groups. Conversely, SAL-derived families (SAL×PAN, SAL×HUA, SAL×NCO) showed high membership to Cluster 3 (yellow), with SAL×PAN being the least admixed and only modest contributions from Cluster 2 across SAL crosses. Cluster 1 contributed minimally overall.
Pairwise fixation index (FST) estimates indicated very low genetic differentiation within each parental group and moderate differentiation between groups (Figure 2 c). Both Kancolla (KAN)- and Salcedo INIA (SAL)-derived families showed minimal internal structuring with FST-values among KAN-NAM families ranging from 0.004 to 0.014 SAL-NAM from 0.004 to 0.005 whereas consistent differentiation was observed in pairwise comparisons between KAN- and SAL-derived families, with an average of 0.15 reflecting a stronger separation by parental origin, and confirming the PCA.






Figure 2: Genetic differentiation of quinoa NAM sub populations. (a) Principal component analysis (PCA) based on genome-wide SNPs. (b) Ancestry estimation for population structure using sparse non-negative matrix factorization (sNMF) at K = 3. (c) Pairwise fixation index (FST) heatmap among NAM subpopulations. For population structure each vertical bar represents an individual, and colors indicate cluster-membership proportions; individuals are grouped by cross: Negra Collana × Kancolla (NCO×KAN), Huariponcho × Kancolla (HUA×KAN), Pasankalla × Kancolla (PAS×KAN), Salcedo INIA × Pandela Rosada (SAL×PAN), Salcedo INIA × Huariponcho (SAL×HUA), and Salcedo INIA × Negra Collana (SAL×NCO).



Genetic diversity indices for the quinoa NAM populations are summarized in Table 1. At the population level, KAN and SAL showed comparable levels of observed heterozygosity (Hₒ = 0.14 in KAN and 0.13 in SAL). Expected heterozygosity (Hₑ) was similar in both populations (0.12 in KAN and 0.11 in SAL). In both cases, observed heterozygosity exceeded expected heterozygosity, resulting in negative inbreeding coefficients (FIS = −0.19 in KAN and −0.21 in SAL), indicating heterozygote excess within the NAM populations.
Across the individual crosses, observed heterozygosity varied between 0.13 and 0.14 across families and consistently exceeded expected heterozygosity (0.10–0.12). As a consequence, all crosses showed negative FIS values, ranging from −0.17 to −0.24. The strongest heterozygote excess was observed in SAL×PAN (FIS = −0.24), followed by NCO×KAN and SAL×HUA (both FIS = −0.21), while HUA×KAN showed the least negative value (FIS = −0.17).
The proportion of polymorphic loci (poly) revealed high levels of genetic variability in the parental populations, with values of 0.95 for KAN and 0.93 for SAL. In contrast, the derived NAM crosses exhibited slightly lower poly values, ranging from 0.67 to 0.76. Among these, PAS×KAN showed the highest proportion of polymorphic loci (0.76), followed by HUA×KAN and NCO×KAN (0.71), whereas SAL-derived crosses such as SAL×HUA, SAL×NCO, and SAL×PAN presented comparatively lower values (0.69, 0.72, and 0.67, respectively).

title: INTRODUCTION
section: Mapping of QTL associated with yield architecture in NAM populations
text:
Mapping of QTL associated with yield architecture in NAM populations
We conducted a genome-wide association study (GWAS) to identify quantitative trait loci (QTLs) associated with key components of quinoa yield architecture across nested association mapping (NAM) families derived from Salcedo INIA (SAL) and Kancolla (KAN), respectively (Figure 3). The phenotypic traits used in the GWAS were analyzed using the best linear unbiased estimates (BLUEs; [50]. Most trait distributions approximated a normal distribution (Supplementary Figure 4), particularly those related to plant architecture and yield components (plant height, panicle length and width, stem diameter, grain yield per plant, and grain yield per plot). In contrast, traits associated with phenology (number of days to 50% flowering and physiological maturity) deviated from normality, reflecting their intrinsic biological nature as time-to-event variables with discrete and often skewed distributions.
GWAS using FarmCPU identified 26 SNPs significantly associated with yield-related traits across the quinoa NAM populations (Figure 3, Supplementary Table 3). Of these, 21 SNPs were detected in the KAN-NAM population and five in the SAL-NAM population. All 26 SNPs exceeded the Bonferroni significance threshold (p < 8 × 10⁻⁶). Phenological traits showed the highest number of associations, with 11 SNPs linked to flowering and maturity time (five for days to 50% flowering and six for days to 50% physiological maturity; Figure 3 a,g). Architectural traits, including plant height and panicle length, accounted for 12 significant associations across developmental stages. In contrast, yield traits were represented by three SNPs associated with grain yield per plot, all of which were population-specific and predominantly identified in the KAN-NAM population (Figure 3). No significant associations were detected for panicle width at maturity or for the panicle width × length trait.
To validate the GWAS signals, QQ plots were examined for each trait (Supplementary Figure 5). The observed distributions of −log₁₀(p) closely followed the expected null distribution across most traits, confirming that the models effectively controlled for population structure and relatedness. Deviations from the null expectation were evident in the tails for flowering time, physiological maturity, panicle length and panicle width, reflecting the presence of true associations rather than spurious signals. In contrast, yield-related traits grain yield per plant, yield per plot and panicle width x length showed only modest departures from expectation, consistent with their lower number of significant SNPs. Together, the Manhattan and QQ plots demonstrate that the detected loci represent reliable associations, especially for phenological traits with strong genetic signals in the KAN-NAM population.
An additional association analysis was performed using the R package NAM, which is specifically designed for nested association mapping populations [51]. The Manhattan plots showed no peaks surpassing the Bonferroni thresholds (Supplementary Figure 6). The QQ plots (Supplementary Figure 7) further confirmed this outcome, as the observed −log₁₀(p) values largely fell below the expected distribution under the null hypothesis, indicating an overall conservative model fit. The NAM implementation did not uncover additional associations beyond those identified with the rMVP package [52].

title: INTRODUCTION
section: Identification of candidate genes associated with significant SNPs
text:
Identification of candidate genes associated with significant SNPs
A total of 68 candidate genes were identified within ±100 kb genomic windows surrounding significant SNPs detected in the GWAS analysis (Supplementary Table 4). Candidate genes were distributed across nine quinoa chromosomes (Supplementary Table 4), with the largest number located on chromosome Cq6A (37 genes), followed by Cq9A (9 genes), Cq5A (8 genes), and Cq2A (5 genes), while fewer genes were detected on Cq7B, Cq8B, Cq3B, Cq5B, and Cq6B. Across traits, the largest number of candidate genes was associated with days to 50% flowering (16 genes) and physiological maturity (14 genes), followed by panicle width (12 genes) and panicle length (12 genes). A smaller number of genes were detected for grain yield per plot (9 genes) and plant height at flowering (5 genes).
For plant height, candidate genes included DIR19 and DIR7, which encode dirigent proteins involved in cell wall formation, together with RPL5, a ribosomal protein associated with cellular growth. For panicle architecture traits, genes such as CRF2, CIP1, and metabolic enzymes including 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase were identified. Phenological traits were associated with genes involved in signaling and transcriptional regulation, including LECRK2 and SR-like splicing factor 1, whereas grain yield per plot was linked to genes related to cellular transport and metabolic regulation such as ABC transporter G family member 3, SNF1-related protein kinase regulatory subunit β3, and VPS32 (Supplementary Table 4).

title: INTRODUCTION
text:
Genomic prediction in NAM population
Assessing genomic prediction performance in structured populations is important for determining the potential use of genomic information in breeding programs and for understanding how population structure may influence predictive ability. To evaluate the potential of genomic prediction in two nested association mapping (NAM) populations, prediction accuracy and normalized root mean square error (NRMSE) were estimated for nine agronomic and yield-related traits. Training and validation datasets were defined using a 60/40 split (n = 125; 60 lines from KAN and 65 from SAL). For each trait, 300 independent iterations were conducted to obtain stable estimates of predictive performance (Figure 4).
The KAN population showed higher predictive performance than SAL across most traits. Mean prediction accuracies averaged across traits were approximately 0.39 in KAN and 0.24 in SAL, indicating differences in predictive capacity between populations. These contrasts were statistically significant (p < 0.001, Supplementary Table 5). Consistent with the accuracy results, NRMSE values were generally lower in KAN than in SAL. For example, mean NRMSE values for days to 50% flowering were 0.75 in KAN and 1.00 in SAL, while days to physiological maturity showed values of 0.76 and 0.97, respectively. Similarly, plant height at maturity presented mean NRMSE values of 0.98 in KAN and 1.02 in SAL. Significant differences between populations were detected for most traits (p < 0.001), with the exception of mean stem diameter at maturity, where NRMSE values were similar between populations (1.02; p = 0.70). For panicle width at maturity, NRMSE values were 1.01 in KAN and 0.98 in SAL, and the difference between populations was significant (p < 0.001).
At the trait level, the highest prediction accuracies in KAN were observed for phenological traits and inflorescence architecture. Days to 50% flowering showed a mean accuracy of 0.80 (range: 0.58–0.93), while days to physiological maturity presented a mean of 0.80 (0.54–0.93). Panicle length at flowering (pnlg_flw) also showed relatively high predictive ability, with a mean accuracy of 0.78 (0.42–0.91). Yield-related traits showed moderate predictive performance in KAN, with mean accuracies of 0.52 (0.07–0.75) for yield per plot and 0.32 (−0.10–0.67) for grain yield per plant.
Predictive performance in the SAL population was generally lower. For example, mean accuracies were approximately 0.28 for panicle length at flowering, 0.34 for panicle length at maturity, and 0.26 for yield per plot, indicating reduced predictive ability under the applied validation scheme. An exception was observed for panicle width at maturity, where SAL showed a higher mean accuracy (0.33) compared with KAN (−0.11), although this difference was not supported by improvements in NRMSE. Mean stem diameter at maturity showed low predictive performance in both populations, with mean accuracies of approximately 0.09 in KAN and −0.06 in SAL.

Mean stem diameter (cm), days to 50% flowering (days), days to 50% physiological maturity (days), plant height (cm) at flowering and maturity, panicle length (cm), panicle width (cm) at flowering and maturity, grain yield per plant (g), panicle width × length (cm2) and yield per plot (g/5m2). Training and validation sets were split in a 60/40 proportion with 60 individuals from the KAN population and 65 from the SAL population (n = 125). For each trait, 300 iterations were performed, and boxplots represent the distributions of prediction accuracy.

title: INTRODUCTION
section: Genetic diversity and population structure in NAM population
text:
Genetic diversity and population structure in NAM population
The assessment of genetic structure and diversity revealed clear differentiation between SAL- and KAN-derived populations, reflecting their divergent breeding histories and adaptation to the environmental conditions of the highland. Salcedo INIA is a high-yielding, disease- and frost-resistant cultivar, while Kancolla is a traditional landrace noted for its stress tolerance and high saponin content [24]. Principal component analysis and ancestry inference consistently separated families according to parental origin, while pairwise FST values confirmed divergence between populations but low differentiation within families (Figure 2). Genetic diversity estimates indicated moderate variability, and consistently negative inbreeding coefficients pointed to a heterozygosity across the populations (Table 1). In the context of the advanced inbreeding generation of the material analyzed (S9), where a high level of homozygosity is expected; however, the residual heterozygosity and negative FIS values reflect the multi-parental origin of the NAM design and the persistence of segregating genomic regions due to recombination among diverse founders.
Patiranage et al. [18] reported low levels of nucleotide diversity (π) in quinoa accessions from highland and lowland populations, with values of 0.000578 and 0.000356, respectively, which is a typical representation of self-pollinated species such as quinoa. These estimates were obtained from high-quality whole-genome resequencing data, which likely provide an accurate representation of the genetic diversity of quinoa than that captured in the present study. In contrast, the present study does not rely on nucleotide diversity estimates but on marker-based diversity using the proportion of polymorphic loci, which reflects allelic variation at the genotyped loci rather than genome-wide sequence diversity. The results obtained in our study showed high proportions of polymorphic loci in the parental lines (Table 1) and moderately reduced in the NAM-derived families, indicating that a considerable fraction of segregating variation was retained across populations (Table 1). KAN-derived crosses tended to exhibit a higher proportion of polymorphic loci values compared to SAL-derived crosses, suggesting a greater contribution or retention of polymorphic segments from the KAN background. Additionally, the relatively narrow range of proportion of polymorphic loci values among crosses indicates a homogeneous distribution of introgressed variation across the NAM population, despite differences in parental origin. This pattern reflects the biparental crossing design and recent recombination events inherent to NAM populations rather than population subdivision.
The high admixture coefficients observed in some KAN- or SAL-derived individuals reflect limited introgression, whereas intermediate coefficients correspond to a greater contribution of alleles from multiple founder parents. Consequently, negative FIS values were detected, indicating an excess of heterozygotes relative to Hardy–Weinberg expectations (Table 1). This pattern likely reflects the biparental crossing design and recent recombination events inherent to NAM populations rather than population subdivision. Additionally, FST estimates revealed differentiation between the SAL- and KAN-derived groups but little divergence within families (Figure 2). In contrast, a study conducted in Colombia that assessed the genetic diversity of quinoa using 27 microsatellite markers across three groups classified according to their geographic origin reported high expected heterozygosity values, ranging from 0.58 to 0.62 [53].

title: INTRODUCTION
text:
QTL for yield-related traits
The genome-wide association analysis identified 26 significant SNPs associated with eight agronomic traits (Figure 3), revealing genomic regions contributing to phenological development, plant architecture, and yield-related traits in quinoa. These traits, including flowering time, plant height, panicle morphology, and grain yield, have previously been identified as key targets for genetic improvement due to their relatively high heritability and direct contribution to yield potential [17,24,54,55]. The detection of multiple loci across traits is consistent with the polygenic architecture of yield formation in quinoa, where complex agronomic traits are controlled by numerous loci with small to moderate effects, as reported in previous QTL and GWAS studies [14].
The detected associations presented an uneven distribution of QTL between NAM subpopulations, with the majority identified in the KAN-derived families. Landraces are known to harbor extensive allelic diversity associated with environmental adaptation, which can increase the probability of detecting trait-associated loci in mapping populations [56]. When comparing the genomic positions of the SNPs detected in this study (SupplementaryTable 3) with loci reported in previous quinoa mapping studies (Supplementary Table 6), several overlapping chromosomal regions were identified, suggesting the presence of conserved genomic regions controlling agronomic traits. In particular, associations were detected on chromosomes Cq5A, Cq6A and Cq9A, which have been implicated in the regulation of phenology, plant architecture, and yield-related traits in quinoa populations [14,57,58].
For phenological traits such as days to 50% flowering and physiological maturity, significant SNPs detected in this study were located on chromosomes including Cq5A, Cq5B, Cq6A, and Cq7B, overlapping with genomic regions previously associated with flowering time in diverse quinoa germplasm panels. Earlier studies have reported QTL controlling flowering time on chromosomes Cq2A, Cq5A, and Cq6A, suggesting that these genomic regions may harbor conserved regulatory elements involved in developmental timing and environmental adaptation [18,59]. The recurrence of associations on these chromosomes across independent studies supports the hypothesis that phenological adaptation in quinoa could be mediated by stable genomic regions maintained across different genetic backgrounds (Supplementary Table 6).
Yield-related traits exhibited fewer significant associations, with SNPs detected mainly on Cq6B and Cq9A. This result is consistent with previous findings indicating that grain yield in quinoa is a highly complex trait influenced by many loci with small effects and strong environmental interactions [59]. The limited number of yield-associated SNPs detected in this study likely reflects both the polygenic nature of yield and the moderate population size typical of NAM populations in emerging crops. Nevertheless, the detection of loci on genomic regions previously linked to yield components reinforces their potential importance for breeding applications.
The genomic regions identified in this study were distributed across several chromosomes, with a notable concentration on Cq6A, Cq5A, and Cq9A, suggesting that key genomic regions contribute trait variation in the quinoa NAM population. Within these regions, candidate genes with biological functions related to the studied traits were identified. Loci associated with plant height were located near genes encoding dirigent proteins (DIR19 and DIR7) and ribosomal proteins, which participate in lignin biosynthesis and cellular growth processes influencing stem elongation and plant architecture [60,61]. For panicle morphology traits, including panicle length and width, candidate genes included cytokinin response factors and metabolic enzymes, which are known to regulate hormonal signaling and developmental processes involved in inflorescence formation [62–64]. For phenological traits, such as flowering time and physiological maturity, candidate genes included receptor-like kinases and RNA splicing factors [65–67], suggesting that signaling pathways and transcriptional regulation may play a role in controlling developmental timing in quinoa. Loci associated with grain yield were located near genes involved in membrane transport and metabolic regulation, including ABC transporters and SNF1-related kinases, highlighting the importance of energy balance and cellular transport processes in yield determination [68–70]. These functional annotations detect genomic associations and provide a preliminary framework for identifying genes underlying agronomic trait variation.
These findings across independent studies reinforces the genetic basis of yield in quinoa is structured by a set of moderate- to large-effect regions stable across populations. These regions could represent strategic targets for marker-assisted selection in breeding programs focused on productivity and climatic adaptation for early maturity.

title: INTRODUCTION
text:
Genomic prediction in NAM populations
Genomic prediction was implemented in the quinoa NAM population to highlight the breeding potential. The simulations showed prediction accuracies ranged from low (-0.16) to high (0.8) across traits and population, demonstrating their application on quinoa. Accuracy distributions in KAN are consistently centered at higher, positive values for phenological and architectural traits (number of days to 50% flowering, number of days to 50% physiological maturity, and panicle length at maturity), whereas in SAL toward low or negative values and display greater dispersion (Figure 4).
The presence of negative prediction accuracies for some traits, particularly in the SAL population, indicates that the genomic model failed to predict phenotypic variation better than random expectation in those cases. Negative correlations between observed phenotypes and predicted GEBVs can arise when training population size is limited, marker density is insufficient, or when the genetic architecture of the trait is highly complex and influenced by environmental variation [48,71]. In this case, the results of the present study could be explained by the relatively small population size and the moderate marker density derived from low-coverage sequencing, which may limit the ability of the model to capture the underlying genetic signal. Such results do not necessarily invalidate the model but rather highlight limitations in prediction power under the current population structure and dataset size.
The results converge on higher model capacity for phenology and inflorescence architecture – particularly in KAN – and moderate performance for yield traits; SAL shows low accuracies and elevated NRMSEs for most traits, with few exceptions and without significant differences where they occur. In addition to prediction accuracy, model performance was evaluated using the normalized root mean square error (NRMSE), which quantifies the magnitude of prediction error relative to the scale of the observed trait values. Lower NRMSE values indicate greater predictive precision and smaller deviations between predicted and observed phenotypes [47,49]. These findings support prioritizing traits such as number of days to 50% flowering, number of days to 50% physiological maturity, and panicle length at maturity, and indicate the need for targeted strategies – e.g., increased sample size, marker enrichment, or multi-environment models – to improve predictability in SAL population.
In our previous study conducted with the same NAM populations, variance components and broad-sense heritability were estimated [24]. Within this context, traits with high heritability, such as days to maturity (H² = 0.95), days to flowering (H² = 0.91), grain width (H² = 0.94), and plant height at maturity (H² = 0.88), also achieved the highest prediction accuracies (i.e. 0.6–0.9), indicating that a substantial proportion of the phenotypic variance is attributable to genetic effects captured by molecular markers. In contrast, traits with intermediate or low heritability, such as plant height at flowering (H² = 0.45), panicle width at flowering (H² = 0.46), and harvest index (H² = 0.72), exhibited lower prediction accuracies (i.e. 0.1–0.4), reflecting a greater contribution of residual variance and genotype × environment interaction. In particular, traits associated with morphological components at early developmental stages showed higher contributions of error varianceₑ and genotype × location variance, which reduces the stability of genetic effects across environments and consequently limits predictive performance [72]. A particularly relevant case was grain yield, which, despite presenting relatively high heritability (H² = 0.84), showed only moderate prediction accuracy (i.e. 0.3–0.5). This discrepancy can be explained by its considerable interaction component genotype × location variance and residual variance, indicating a complex, likely polygenic genetic architecture.
These differences between populations likely reflect contrasting genetic architectures and trait heritabilities between highland cultivars and traditional landraces backgrounds [24]. Importantly, high prediction accuracies were achieved despite moderate marker density and low sequencing depth, producing outcomes consistent with results in other cereals and legumes [44,46]. The findings confirm that genomic prediction can be implemented in quinoa breeding pipelines to accelerate genetic gain. Even if we used the two stage approach for the analysis [40]. The integration of genomic prediction under multi-environment trials is particularly relevant, as it allows for the explicit modeling of genotype × environment interactions, which play a key role in determining yield stability across environments [73].
The observed prediction accuracies indicate that genomic prediction can be effectively implemented in quinoa NAM populations, particularly for phenological and architectural traits. The higher predictive performance detected in the KAN population suggests that genetic background and population structure influence model efficiency, highlighting the importance of population-specific training in genomic selection frameworks. Our results demonstrate the practical applicability of genomic selection in quinoa and highlight its potential to enhance selection strategies in Andean germplasm.

title: INTRODUCTION
text:
Limitations and perspectives
Despite the results, some limitations of the study must be acknowledged. The sequencing depth (~1× coverage) limited marker density. Although genotype imputation can improve low coverage datasets, its accuracy depends on the availability of a suitable reference panel, which is currently unavailable for Peruvian Highlands quinoa [74]. Therefore, we used stringent quality filtering of directly observed SNPs to ensure robust downstream analyses. Future studies using higher sequencing depth or improved reference panels will further enhance mapping resolution [75]. The number of parental lines in this quinoa NAM population is smaller than in classical designs such as the original maize NAM population [76], which included 25 founders crossed to a single reference line. The reduced number of individuals per population could decrease the statistical power for GWAS and genomic prediction analyses. Nevertheless, the smaller population size is offset by the high genetic divergence between parental lines, ensuring allelic diversity for effective QTL detection.
Unlike our previous study [24], which focused on phenotypic characterization and quantitative genetic analyses of these populations, the present work integrates those published phenotypic data with newly generated genome-wide marker information to investigate the genetic architecture of agronomic traits through a NAM framework. The field evaluations were restricted to two highland sites in Puno, which limited the exploration of genotype × environment interactions on inter-Andean valley or coastal ecological regions of Peru [24]. The NAM populations were derived from four different founders and still represent only a fraction of the genetic base available in the Andes. Future research should explore advanced modeling approaches, including deep learning architectures tailored to small datasets, to enhance genomic prediction accuracy [44]. While prediction accuracies were encouraging, they should be interpreted cautiously due to relatively small training population sizes. Larger training sets and integration of advanced modeling approaches such as deep learning may further enhance predictive power [44,71].
Genome-wide LD was evaluated separately for the SAL and KAN NAM subpopulations. Although LD decreased slightly within the shortest physical distances, r2 rapidly reached a low background level and remained nearly constant across larger distances. This pattern is consistent with the advanced recombinant inbred structure of the quinoa NAM populations, in which repeated selfing and accumulated recombination substantially reduce long-range linkage disequilibrium while increasing mapping resolution [77,78]. Therefore, a conventional genome-wide LD decay curve did not provide additional biological information for interpreting the association analyses.

This instructions are designed for the management, organization, and utilization of images for annotation processes in image analysis projects. The following guidelines must be observed:

All images must be placed in the library folder.

The script code contains the instructions for moving images in blocks.

It is necessary to ensure that images are not duplicated and are properly rotated before use.
The website associated with this repository will display only the content defined in the _quarto.yml.

The website must be built using the command:
quarto render website

The library folder will be hosted on the website, and each image will be assigned a unique URL.
Image URLs can be extracted using the code provided in Image URL for Label Studio.
The generated links should be employed as references for annotations in Label Studio.



3 Change or fix image path

library(tidyverse)
library(magick)

imgdir <- choose.dir() 
newdir <- choose.dir() 

imgfiles <- list.files(path = imgdir
                       , full.names = T
                       , recursive = T
                       )

movefiles <- imgfiles %>% 
  enframe(name = "num", value = "path") %>% 
  mutate(imgname = gsub('.*GERM/(.+)', '\\1', path)) %>% 
  mutate(across(imgname, ~gsub('/', '_', .))) %>% 
  mutate(across(imgname, ~gsub('[[:space:]]', '-', .))) %>% 
  mutate(across(imgname, ~gsub('\\(|\\)', '_', .))) %>% 
  mutate(across(imgname, ~gsub('__', '_', .))) %>% 
  mutate(newdir = file.path({{newdir}}, imgname)) %>% 
  filter(str_detect(imgname, "DIA-(3|4)")) %>% 
  filter(!str_detect(imgname, "mp4"))

nrow(movefiles)

walk(movefiles, \(x) {
  
  file.copy(from = movefiles$path, to = movefiles$newdir
            , overwrite = T)
})



4 Image URL for Label Studio

newdir <- "library/maiz/"

imgs <- list.files(path = newdir
                   , pattern = "jpg"
                   , full.names = TRUE
                   , recursive = TRUE
                   ) %>% 
  enframe() %>% 
  mutate(url = file.path("https://flavjack.github.io/pheno-germination", value))

imgs %>% 
  select(url) %>% 
  write_csv(file.path(newdir, "images4labelstudio.txt"), col_names = F)
